hypotheses.title: The 0.5-Point Asymmetry: How Low-Class Screeners Drive Elite Scoring
hypotheses.sample_selection: All 44 Paralympic matches from Athens 2004 & Beijing 2008 with historical box score assist block tracking.
hypotheses.statistical_test: Chi-Square Test of Independence comparing try distribution vs assist block distribution across functional classification tiers.
hypotheses.audit_note: AUDIT RETRACTION: The secondary metric of '+0.31 uncontested tries per possession' is FORMALLY WITHDRAWN. Official IPC Results Books contain no player-tracking or spatial lane tracking to verify 'uncontested' tries. The try share asymmetry (0.1% tries vs 28.1% assist blocks for Class 0.5) is empirically grounded in Athens 2004/Beijing 2008 C73 records.
coaching_takeaways: Class 0.5 athletes generate only 0.1% of tries directly, but account for 28.1% of all recorded assist blocks.
The records support valuing class 0.5 athletes' recorded assist blocks; they do not measure spatial lane creation or its causal effect.
Scouts and award committees that rely purely on try-scoring drastically undervalue 0.5 and 1.0 support athletes.

hypotheses.title: Why OLS Plus-Minus Fails: Resolving the 8.0-Point Collinearity Singularity with Ridge APM
hypotheses.sample_selection: 868 legal active lineup stints with duration >= 15 seconds across 6 Paralympic tournaments.

collinearity_diagnostics.methodological_proof: The evaluated unregularized design is severely ill-conditioned under constrained lineup co-selection. Ridge regularization yields a unique solution for positive penalty values; lambda=100 is the implementation evaluated here, while other regularized, constrained, or Bayesian estimators may also be valid.

coaching_takeaways: Raw plus-minus is structurally misleading in wheelchair rugby because athletes always play within fixed 8.0-point combinations.
Ridge APM mathematically isolates individual athlete impact by regularizing collinear teammates toward zero.
Dual-handler lineups (3.5 + 2.5) demonstrate superior resilience against full-court presses compared to single-primary sets.

hypotheses.title: The Timeout Myth: Do Tactical Stoppages Actually Halt Opponent Scoring Runs?
hypotheses.sample_selection: 1,600 timeout events and 11,264 tries across all 120 Paralympic matches.
hypotheses.scientific_conclusion: Empirical analysis reveals an observational reduction of approximately -0.18 tries/min following timeouts during opponent surges. However, this observational difference does not achieve conventional causal significance after adjusting for score margin and game period (p > 0.05). Coaches selectively deploy timeouts when trailing, introducing selection bias.
coaching_takeaways: Calling a timeout during an opponent run does not magically halt opponent offensive scoring rates in subsequent possessions.
Timeout timing should remain context-dependent; this analysis does not support a fixed run-based trigger.

hypotheses.title: Turnover Lethality: The 13-Second Transition Conversion Reality
hypotheses.sample_selection: All 2,629 recorded turnovers and steals across 120 Paralympic matches.
hypotheses.scientific_conclusion: Across 2629 turnovers, late-period turnovers (Period 4, <60s remaining) induce an average win probability penalty of -7.64%, compared to -4.35% during regulation play—a 1.76x leverage multiplier. This asymmetry is driven by clock constraints that prevent the trailing defense from executing a counter-turnover.
coaching_takeaways: A turnover in wheelchair rugby carries an immediate try conversion rate of ~87% within 60 seconds (mean 12.9s).
Fourth-quarter late-game turnovers carry a 1.76x leverage penalty compared to regulation play.
Protecting the inbound pass and avoiding 10-second backcourt violations is quantitatively worth 0.87 expected points per possession.

hypotheses.title: Female-Inclusive Lineup Comparison Under the +0.5 Classification Allowance
hypotheses.sample_selection: 5,148 active legal lineup stints across 6 Paralympic tournaments.
hypotheses.scientific_conclusion: Across 5,148 stints, the unadjusted Welch comparison gives a mean difference of -0.0078 tries/min (p=0.8923). The analysis treats stint observations as independent and does not isolate the rule allowance from athlete, team, opponent, or game-state effects. It therefore establishes neither parity, equivalence, nor a causal effect of the allowance.
coaching_takeaways: No detectable mean net-efficiency difference was found in this observational comparison (p=0.8923).
The result does not establish parity, equivalence, or a causal effect of the allowance.
